object.medium: Live slow-scan television, 320 lines at 10 frames a second, scan-converted for broadcast; shown as a silent loop from NASA's 2009 restoration
object.description: At 02:56 UTC on 21 July 1969 Neil Armstrong stepped off the footpad of the Lunar Module Eagle onto the Sea of Tranquility, and about 600 million people watched him do it. The pictures came from a small Westinghouse camera mounted upside down on a fold-down equipment bay on the lander's side, which Armstrong released by pulling a lanyard as he climbed down the ladder. It transmitted a slow-scan signal of 320 lines at ten frames a second, received at Goldstone in California and at Honeysuckle Creek and Parkes in Australia, where it was converted for broadcast by pointing an ordinary television camera at a monitor. That double conversion, and the harsh lunar light, give the famous ghostly image. The original slow-scan tapes were later reused and lost; in 2009 NASA gathered the best surviving broadcast recordings and had them cleaned up, and that restoration is what is shown here. Armstrong's words as he stepped down, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind', are the most quoted sentence of the twentieth century.
facts: Armstrong said he intended 'one small step for a man'; the 'a' is not audible in the recording.
The Lunar Module camera had a single 7-pound body, two lenses and no viewfinder; the astronauts aimed it by hand after the first steps.
Buzz Aldrin followed Armstrong down the ladder nineteen minutes later; Michael Collins, orbiting above, could not see the broadcast at all.
The moonwalk lasted two hours and thirty-one minutes and the two men never went more than about sixty metres from the lander.

tour: The first step on the Moon, 21 July 1969, as six hundred million people saw it on television. It plays as you come close.
